citation.title: Inference in Spatial Experiments with Interference using the SpatialEffect Package
citation.venue: Journal of Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics

standing_assumptions:
(S1) Setting [Section 2.1, p. 141 (PDF p. 4)]. “Specifically, suppose that we have a set of intervention nodes indexed by $i = 1, ..., N$, and these nodes are arrayed as points in a spatial field, $\mathcal{X}$. Each point in this spatial field, $x \in \mathcal{X}$, equals a coordinate vector of length 2 (recording, e.g., longitude and latitude coordinates). For point interventions, the coordinates of an intervention node $i$ can be given by $x(i)$.” “For each intervention node, we have a binary random variable $Z_i \in \{0, 1\}$ that connotes whether, at node $i$, treatment is activated ($Z_i = 1$) or not ($Z_i = 0$). Denote the ordered vector of random treatment assignments as $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, ..., Z_N)'$, with support $\mathcal{Z}$. We define potential outcomes such that at each point $x \in \mathcal{X}$, we would have outcome $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ when the treatment assignment is such that $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}$, and these potential outcomes are defined for each $\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}$. We stress that outcomes are defined at all $x$ values in $\mathcal{X}$, not just at the $x(i)$ values, which makes the setting bipartite.” “The outcome that we observe at point $x$, labeled $Y_x$, is the potential outcome associated with the realized treatment assignment vector: $Y_x = \sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \mathcal{Z}} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\mathbf{1}(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z})$, where $\mathbf{1}(\cdot)$ is the indicator function.” “(i.e., we allow for effects to be nonlinear and heterogenous).” Points and polygons [p. 141]: “these intervention nodes could be points or polygons. Wang et al. (2022) show that the analysis is essentially the same, and so for illustration here we will focus on point interventions.”

(S2) Design [Section 2.1, p. 142 (PDF p. 5)]. “Our analysis focuses on randomized experiments for which the distribution of the treatment assignment vector, $\mathbf{Z}$, is known. Our inferential results are derived from the treatment assignment distribution. Extensions to observational studies would follow if the treatment assignment mechanism resembled the kind of Bernoulli process assumed in Wang et al. (2022).” [Section 2.2, p. 142] “$\alpha$ is the experimental design parameter that governs the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ (that is, the probabilities of different treatment assignment vectors), $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is a vector of treatment values at nodes other than node $i$, and $\mathcal{Z}_{-i}$ is the set of possible values that $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ can take. The design parameter, $\alpha$, is an abbreviated way of capturing a variety of factors that might affect the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$. For example, it could index vectors of treatment assignment probabilities for the intervention nodes, where such probabilities would determine the level of treatment saturation. It could also index the correlation structure for the treatments, which would characterize potential restrictions (for example, stratification or clustering) on the profiles of possible treatment assignments.”

(S3) Marginalized outcomes and point effects [Section 2.2, p. 142 (PDF p. 5)]. “we rewrite the potential outcome at point $x$ as $Y_x(Z_i, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ is the treatment status of all the intervention nodes except for node $i$. To concentrate on the effect generated by node $i$, we hold node $i$ to treatment value $z$ and marginalize over this variation in $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ to define an “individualistic” average of potential outcomes at point $x$: $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}\left[Y_x(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})\right] = \sum_{\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}} Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})\Pr(\mathbf{Z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}_{-i}; \alpha)$.” “This allows us to define the causal effect at point $x$ of intervening on node $i$, allowing other nodes to vary as they otherwise would under $\alpha$: $\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = Y_{ix}(1;\alpha) - Y_{ix}(0,\alpha)$.” (The comma in the last term is the paper's.)

(S4) Circle averages and the AMR [Section 2.2, p. 143 (PDF p. 6)]. “$\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$, where $d_i(x) = ||x(i) - x||$ is some well-defined metric that defines whether point $x$ is within a specified distance from intervention node $i$, which is located at $x(i)$, and $\zeta$ is a suitable integration measure.” “$\mu_i(z; d, \alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i}); d)]$ is the potential $d$-radius circle average around node $i$, given that node $i$ is assigned to treatment condition $z$ and marginalizing over possible assignments to other points.” “$\tau_i(d; \alpha) = \mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)$, is the average of individualistic responses for points along the circle of radius $d$ around node $i$.” The AMR for distance $d$ is denoted $\tau(d;\alpha)$; its display is misprinted (P008-T14 gives it as printed and corrected): $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha)$.

(S5) Estimator [Section 2.3, pp. 143–144 (PDF pp. 6–7)]. “the preferred estimator for practical purposes is the Hajek estimator (Särndal et al. 1992, pp. 182-184), given by: $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d) = \frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d) - \frac{1}{N_0}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(1 - Z_i)\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ where $N_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{N} Z_i$ and $N_0 = N - N_1$.” Here $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}; d)$ is the circle average of the observed outcomes.

(S6) Hypotheses and the two inference methods [Section 2.3, p. 144 (PDF p. 7)]. “The sharp null hypothesis states that the interventions have no effects whatsoever, such that $Y_x(\mathbf{Z}) = Y_x(\mathbf{0})$ , in which case all unit-level effects are also zero and the AMR is zero. If one assumes that the sharp null hypothesis holds, then the randomization distribution of the AMR can be simulated by simply permuting treatment assignment, estimating the AMR under each of these permutations, and then collecting the resulting set of estimates (Imbens and Rubin 2015, Ch. 5). The resulting distribution is referred to as the null permutation distribution.” The weak null hypothesis is “that the AMR equals zero”. The second method “provides confidence intervals that combine a normal approximation with a nonparametric spatial heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (spatial-HAC) standard error estimator as proposed by Conley (1999).”

(S7) Package conventions [Section 3, pp. 145–146 (PDF pp. 8–9)]. [p. 145] “Users can choose a set of points that form the edge of a circle of radius $d$, that form a circular band (“donut”) centered at radius $d$, or that form a sector centered at $d$ (“disk”), by altering the option cType. When ras_Z is provided, the distance will be calculated from the boundary of each polygon and we implement polygon intervention. Otherwise, it is calculated from the center of each intervention node and point intervention is implemented.” [p. 145] “For the asymptotic variance estimator, users need to specify a distance threshold (cutoff) beyond which interference dependence does not exist.” [p. 146] “For a specified error rate of $\delta$ (e.g., $\delta = 0.05$), it is the $\delta/2$ and $1-\delta/2$ percentiles of the sharp null distribution generated by permutation. At each distance $d$, the sharp null hypothesis of no effect is rejected if the AMR estimate is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1 - \delta/2$ percentile.” [p. 146] “The SpatialEffectTest() function generates the null permutation distribution of the sum of the AMR estimates within the specified range.”

(S8) Toy example [Sections 4–5, pp. 146–150 (PDF pp. 9–13)]. “The toy example includes 4 intervention nodes in a spatial field where outcomes are recorded in a 4-by-4 raster (left plot of Fig. 2).” “We suppose Bernoulli random assignment of the nodes to treatment, in which case there are 16 ways treatment could be applied, all with equal probability.” [pp. 147–148] “we choose dVec to be a sequence from 0.1 to 2 with an interval length of 0.1. The cutoff point for the spatial HAC variance is set to be 0.4 and the number of permutations is set to be 1000.” Footnote 5 [p. 148]: “The number doesn't make any difference here as there are in total 6 assignments.” (The six assignments are those with two of the four nodes treated, as in the observed assignment.)

(S9) Points the paper leaves open, fixed here so that the targets are definite (these are conventions of this file, not statements of the paper). (i) The paper does not say how a “quantile” or “percentile” of a finite permutation distribution is computed. The staged implementations call R's quantile() with its default rule (type 7): for order statistics $x_{(1)} \le \dots \le x_{(n)}$ and $q \in [0,1]$, with $h = 1 + (n-1)q$, $j = \lfloor h \rfloor$ and $g = h - j$, $Q_7(q) = (1-g)x_{(j)} + g\,x_{(j+1)}$ (and $Q_7(1) = x_{(n)}$). The printed toy percentiles $\mp 7.97$ are reproduced by this rule and lie strictly inside the range of the six enumerated values. (ii) $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ uses $Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})$ for every $\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}$ and both $z \in \{0,1\}$; a statement below that uses it assumes potential outcomes are defined at each such argument (for instance on all of $\{0,1\}^N$). (iii) $\mathcal{Z}$ is finite, so every expectation over $\mathbf{Z}$ is a finite sum. For a finite set of outcome points with counting measure the circle average is the arithmetic mean over the points with $d_i(x) = d$; every example below is of this kind or has outcomes constant on the circles concerned. (iv) The paper has no numbered results, no appendix and no proofs; every target is an unnumbered statement or display, located by page.

Scope of the list. The paper is a tutorial with no numbered results and no proofs. Three of its eight headline claims contain mathematical statements and enter as headline targets: P008-H1 (the definition of the AMR and its circle-average identities, P008-T25), P008-H2 (the sharp and weak null hypotheses, P008-T26, and the attributed consistency and normality statement, P008-T28) and P008-H6 (the additive case of the attributed equivalence with a structural coefficient, P008-T27). P008-H3, P008-H4 and P008-H5 are a simulated illustration, an empirical estimate and its interpretation; P008-H7 and P008-H8 describe the method and the package. Twelve confirmed errors have corrections that change a mathematical statement, a formula or a constant and are targets: P008-N012 (Major; the reference law of the Uganda permutation test), P008-E002 (Moderate; the percentile rule and the toy example's rejection), P008-N002 (Moderate; the toy example's cutoff), P008-N016 (Moderate; the sum of AMR estimates read as a change in a probability), P008-E015 (Moderate; the bandwidth formula of the archived variance code), P008-E003 (Minor; 12.38 for 8.00), P008-E004 (Minor; the step 5/111 for 0.5/111), P008-E005 (Minor; the misprinted display of the AMR), P008-E007 (Minor; the band described as a set of intervention nodes), P008-N001 (Minor; the band as described and as implemented), P008-N004 (Minor; the scale of the effect function in Figure 2) and P008-N009 (Minor; what the estimate at distance 0 averages). P008-E015, P008-N001, P008-N004 and P008-N009 set a sentence or figure of the article against the staged package or vignette, which is a later snapshot than the release the article cites; they are listed because each rests on an exact formal example or derivation and its correction replaces a formula, a constant or the description of the set that is averaged, and each target says which premise is read from source code and lies outside what Lean can establish. The other nine confirmed errors are not targets because their corrections change no mathematical statement: P008-N017 (Moderate) is the horizontal placement of the band estimates in the bottom panel of Figure 8, established by recalculation from archived data (the band convention on which it rests is P008-T17 (b)); P008-E006 is an argument name; P008-E009 and P008-E012 concern the typesetting of the printed calls, an input guard of the later package and the wording of a numerical default; P008-N006 and P008-N007 concern the reproducibility of the toy intervals and of the smoothed curve with the staged copies of the package; P008-N005 is the colour key of Figure 3; P008-E010 is copy-editing (the mathematical content of the garbled sentence of p. 144 is in P008-T3, P008-T4 and P008-T22); P008-E011 is bibliographic. Findings classed as a clarity note (P008-E008), as not confirmed (P008-E001, P008-N003, P008-N013), as undetermined (P008-N008, P008-N010, P008-N011, P008-N014, P008-N015) or as out of scope (P008-E013, P008-E014) are outside the brief.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, “the starting point at 0 corresponds to the area within the boundary of each village”, corrected: the value at distance 0 averages over the village boundary
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] “Therefore, the starting point at 0 corresponds to the area within the boundary of each village.”

[Corrected; Sol's smallest repair] “For the edge-based estimates, the value at distance 0 averages outcomes over raster cells on the village boundary, rather than over the full village polygon. The smoothed curve is fitted to these boundary-based summaries across distances.”

[Formal content]
(a) [Discrete form, as computed.] For a rasterized polygon with cell set $R$, let $\partial R \subseteq R$ be its boundary cells (the cells of $R$ with at least one of their eight neighbouring cells outside $R$). The edge summary at distance 0 is $\frac{1}{|\partial R|}\sum_{x \in \partial R} Y_x$ and the within-polygon summary is $\frac{1}{|R|}\sum_{x \in R} Y_x$. For a $5 \times 5$ block of cells, $|R| = 25$, $|\partial R| = 16$ and $R \setminus \partial R$ is the central $3 \times 3$ block.
(b) [Continuous form, under the paper's own definitions.] With the distance of a point $x$ to polygon $P_i$ “calculated from the boundary” (p. 145), $d_i(x) = \inf_{y \in \partial P_i}\|x - y\|$, the set $\{x : d_i(x) = 0\}$ over which the edge average at $d = 0$ is taken (S4) is the boundary $\partial P_i$ itself; it contains no interior point of $P_i$, and every interior point $x$ of $P_i$ has $d_i(x) > 0$.
(c) [The two summaries are different functionals.] There are outcomes for which they differ: in the example of P008-T19 the edge contrast at distance 0 is $0$ and the within-polygon contrast is $9/25$ (as AMRs: $0$ and $9/50$).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)–(S5): the spatial field $\mathcal{X}$, the nodes $x(i)$, the assignment $\mathbf{Z}$ with support $\mathcal{Z}$, potential outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ (p. 141); $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ and $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ (p. 142); $d_i(x)$, $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$, $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$, $\tau(d;\alpha)$ (p. 143); $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$, $N_1$, $N_0$ (p. 144). Polygon interventions and the edge selection: P008-T19. $\partial P_i$ is the topological boundary of the closed polygon $P_i \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, nonempty and closed.
canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair for P008-N009 in validated.json and the validator's derivation.md, sections 1–3 and 5. Parts (a) and (c) are the validator's. Part (b) was written when this target was fixed: it is the continuous counterpart of the validator's observation that Section 3 of the article describes distance from the polygon boundary and defines no exception at zero for the edge estimator; it follows from the closedness of the boundary and from the interior and the boundary being disjoint. The zero-distance value of the smoothed curve was not recomputed by the validator. The 1–2.5 km test does not involve distance 0.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 6, the test of the cumulative effect between 1 and 2.5 km and its conclusion “thus significant with $p < 0.05$”, as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. [p. 151] “The study was carried out in 121 villages, 60 of which were randomly assigned to treatment (Fig. 6).” [p. 145] “The permutation test can be adjusted to account for blocking or clustering in experimental design.” [p. 153] “We test whether the cumulative effect between 1 and 2.5 kilometers are statistically significant using the SpatialEffectTest() function:” testResult <- SpatialEffectTest(AMRest, test.range = c(1/111, / 2.5/111)) (“/” marks a line break of the paper) “For the cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km, the 0.025 and .975 percentiles of the sharp null permutation distribution are $-0.0304$ and $0.0336$ (that is, a 3.04 percentage point reduction to a 3.36 percentage point increase in the cumulative probability of forest loss), respectively. The estimated cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km is $-0.0321$ (i.e., a 3.21 percentage point reduction). The cumulative effect between 1 km and 2.5 km is thus significant with $p < 0.05$. Beyond 2.5 km, spillover effects of the PES program appear to be negligible.” “Thus, we find evidence for a spatial bandwagon effect that emanates up to 2.5 km outward beyond the intervention sites.”

Formal content touched by the finding: (i) $-0.0321 < -0.0304$ (true); (ii) the inference from (i) to “$p < 0.05$” by the rule of p. 146 (reject when the statistic is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1 - \delta/2$ percentile, $\delta = 0.05$), which presumes that $-0.0304$ and $0.0336$ are the 0.025 and 0.975 percentiles of the distribution of the cumulative statistic under the law by which the 121 villages were assigned, the sharp null holding.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)–(S5): the spatial field $\mathcal{X}$, the nodes $x(i)$, the assignment $\mathbf{Z}$ with support $\mathcal{Z}$, potential outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ (p. 141); $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ and $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ (p. 142); $d_i(x)$, $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$, $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$, $\tau(d;\alpha)$ (p. 143); $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$, $N_1$, $N_0$ (p. 144). The sharp null and the null permutation distribution: (S6). The rejection rule and the cumulative statistic: (S7).
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, for a finding rated Major. Not refuted as a numerical statement: the validator records false_as_printed as undetermined (null), because the percentiles, the statistic and the p-value were not reconstructed and the test under the documented design could still reject. What fails is the support for (ii): the printed calls generate unrestricted permutations, which is not the documented design (P008-T1, P008-T2). Three other findings touch the same passage: the grid as printed has no point in the range (P008-E004; P008-T12, P008-T13); the interpolated-percentile rule is not calibrated in general (P008-E002; P008-T3, P008-T4); the percentage-point gloss (P008-N016; P008-T7, P008-T8, P008-T24). A formalization should confine itself to (i) and to the conditional form of (ii) given in P008-T2 (a).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Sections 2.3, 3 and 5, the percentile rule for the sharp-null permutation test and the toy example's rejection at $\delta = 0.05$, as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. [p. 144] “For a two-way test of the sharp null hypothesis for a specific AMR value with an error rate of $\delta$, one can evaluate the estimated AMR relative to the $\delta/2$ and $1 - \delta/2$ quantiles of the null permutation distribution. (We use $\delta$ for the inferential error rate here so as not to confuse with $\alpha$, which is defined above to characterize the experimental design.) Such tests of the sharp null are approximately in exact finite samples, where the quality of the approximation depends the extent to the which the simulated permutations cover the full set of possible permutations. We can also use a permutation test to test linear functionals of the AMR, such as the mean or cumulative AMR within a range of distance values. To do so, one evaluates the estimated AMR functional value against the null permutation distribution of the functional values.” [p. 146] “For a specified error rate of $\delta$ (e.g., $\delta = 0.05$), it is the $\delta/2$ and $1-\delta/2$ percentiles of the sharp null distribution generated by permutation.” “At each distance $d$, the sharp null hypothesis of no effect is rejected if the AMR estimate is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1 - \delta/2$ percentile.” [p. 148, footnote 5] “The number doesn't make any difference here as there are in total 6 assignments.” [p. 149] “The results suggest that the AMR estimates are marginally significant when $d$ is small, where the estimates are slightly larger than the .975 percentile of the sharp null permutation distribution and the red line on the bottom is close to be positive.” [pp. 149–150] “The 0.025 and .975 percentiles of the sharp null permutation distribution of the cumulative effect are $-7.97$ and $7.97$, respectively, while the actual cumulative effect is 12.38. Based on an error rate of $\delta = 0.05$, we would reject the sharp null hypothesis that there is no cumulative effect on the distance interval of $[0.1, 0.5]$.”

Formal content touched by the finding: (i) the rule “reject the sharp null when the statistic is smaller than the $\delta/2$ percentile or larger than the $1-\delta/2$ percentile of the null permutation distribution” has error rate $\delta$, exactly so when the permutations cover all possible assignments; (ii) in the toy example, with six assignments, percentiles $-7.97$ and $7.97$ and statistic $12.38$, the sharp null is rejected at error rate $\delta = 0.05$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)–(S5): the spatial field $\mathcal{X}$, the nodes $x(i)$, the assignment $\mathbf{Z}$ with support $\mathcal{Z}$, potential outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ (p. 141); $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ and $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ (p. 142); $d_i(x)$, $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$, $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$, $\tau(d;\alpha)$ (p. 143); $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$, $N_1$, $N_0$ (p. 144). The sharp null and the null permutation distribution: (S6). The cumulative statistic: (S7). The toy design: (S8). The quantile rule of the implementation: (S9)(i).
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, for a finding rated Moderate. (i) is refuted for the interpolated percentiles that the toy example uses (P008-T3) and (ii) is refuted for every deterministic rule on six equally likely assignments (P008-T4 (a)); the statistic 12.38 is itself a misprint for 8.00 (P008-T11). (i) is not refuted for quantile rules with calibrated discrete critical values (P008-T4 (b)). The phrase “approximately in exact finite samples” also carries a copy-editing slip (P008-E010), which is not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 3, the instruction on the spatial-HAC cutoff, and the toy example's intervals “based on the spatial-HAC standard errors” with cutoff 0.4, as printed
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. [p. 145] “For the asymptotic variance estimator, users need to specify a distance threshold (cutoff) beyond which interference dependence does not exist. This can be based on substantive judgments about the likely spatial extent of interference, and can be varied as part of a sensitivity analysis.” [pp. 147–148] “The cutoff point for the spatial HAC variance is set to be 0.4 and the number of permutations is set to be 1000.” [p. 148] “Conley.CI.l and Conley.CI.u refer to the lower and upper bounds of the confidence intervals based on the spatial HAC variance estimator.” [p. 149, table] dVec, AMR_est, Conley.CI.l, Conley.CI.u, Per.CI.l, Per.CI.u: [1,] 0.1, 1.491, -0.277, 3.259, -1.566, 1.566; [2,] 0.2, 1.550, -0.242, 3.343, -1.626, 1.626; [3,] 0.3, 1.550, -0.242, 3.343, -1.626, 1.626; [4,] 0.4, 1.691, -0.050, 3.431, -1.666, 1.666; [5,] 0.5, 1.714, -0.020, 3.448, -1.684, 1.684; [6,] 0.6, 1.700, -0.038, 3.438, -1.673, 1.673; [7,] 0.7, 1.678, -0.066, 3.422, -1.657, 1.657; [8,] 0.8, 1.002, -0.067, 2.071, -1.005, 1.005; [9,] 0.9, -0.816, -2.424, 0.791, -1.328, 1.328; [10,] 1.0, -0.791, -2.295, 0.714, -1.307, 1.307. [p. 149] “The red dotted line is the 95% confidence interval based on the spatial-HAC standard errors.” [p. 153] “The cutoff is set at 10 km = 10,000 m.” “When cutoff equals 0, the confidence intervals ignore the uncertainties caused by interference. Hence, they are much narrower compared to the others.”

Formal content touched by the finding: (i) [the instruction] if the node-level contributions $\phi_i$, $\phi_j$ to the contrast are uncorrelated whenever the distance $D_{ij}$ between nodes $i$ and $j$ exceeds the cutoff $c$, then $\sum_{i,j}\mathrm{Cov}(\phi_i, \phi_j)\mathbf{1}\{D_{ij} \le c\} = \mathrm{Var}\left(\sum_i \phi_i\right)$; (ii) [the toy illustration] the intervals in the columns Conley.CI.l and Conley.CI.u, computed with cutoff 0.4, are intervals that account for the dependence between nodes caused by interference, unlike intervals with cutoff 0.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)–(S5): the spatial field $\mathcal{X}$, the nodes $x(i)$, the assignment $\mathbf{Z}$ with support $\mathcal{Z}$, potential outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ (p. 141); $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ and $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ (p. 142); $d_i(x)$, $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$, $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$, $\tau(d;\alpha)$ (p. 143); $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$, $N_1$, $N_0$ (p. 144). The spatial-HAC interval: (S6). The cutoff: (S7). The toy example: (S8). $\phi_i$ and the uniform-kernel spatial-HAC variance: P008-T6.
canonical_claim.note: The statement as printed, for a finding rated Moderate. (i) is true (it is an identity) and is the reading under which the validators find the instruction correct as printed. (ii) fails: with cutoff 0.4 no pair of distinct toy nodes is within the cutoff, so the printed limits are the limits with cutoff 0 (P008-T6 (a), (b)), which the paper's own sentence on p. 153 describes as ignoring the uncertainty caused by interference; and positive covariances between the contributions of distinct nodes are omitted (the validators certify $a_{ij}a_{ji} > 0$ for all six pairs at $d = 0.1$ in the reconstructed toy example). The same sentence of p. 145 is the article passage touched by P008-E015 (P008-T9, P008-T10). Each printed interval is symmetric about its estimate to the printed precision.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 2.2: the average marginalized response and the two circle-average identities (“$\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$ is simply the circle average of the $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ values”; $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$ “is the circle average of the $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ values”), with the rule of Section 4 for computing $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ in the toy example
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 142] “$Y_{ix}(z;\alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}\left[Y_x(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i})\right] = \sum_{\mathbf{z}_{-i} \in \mathcal{Z}_{-i}} Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})\Pr(\mathbf{Z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}_{-i}; \alpha)$”; “$\tau_{ix}(\alpha) = Y_{ix}(1;\alpha) - Y_{ix}(0,\alpha)$. This defines the effect on raster cell $x$ of switching node $i$ from no treatment to active treatment, averaging over possible treatment assignments to the nodes other than $i$.” [Printed, p. 143] “$\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} Y_x(\mathbf{z})\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$”; “Then, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha) = \mathrm{E}_{\mathbf{Z}_{-i}}[\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(z, \mathbf{Z}_{-i}); d)]$ is the potential $d$-radius circle average around node $i$, given that node $i$ is assigned to treatment condition $z$ and marginalizing over possible assignments to other points. The quantity $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$ is simply the circle average of the $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ values. Finally, $\tau_i(d;\alpha) = \mu_i(1; d, \alpha) - \mu_i(0; d, \alpha)$, is the average of individualistic responses for points along the circle of radius $d$ around node $i$. This is the circle average of the $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ values for outcome at distance $d$ from intervention node $i$.” “Working with these terms, our target quantity is the average marginalized response (AMR) for distance $d$, which is simply the average $d$-radius effect over the intervention nodes: $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\tau_i(d;\alpha)\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\bar{\mu}_i(1; d, \alpha) - \bar{\mu}_i(0; d, \alpha)\right]$.” (The display is misprinted; P008-T14.) [Printed, p. 146] “We suppose Bernoulli random assignment of the nodes to treatment, in which case there are 16 ways treatment could be applied, all with equal probability.” [Printed, p. 147] “This corresponds to the difference in mean potential outcomes when node $i$ is in treatment versus in control, where these means are taken with respect to the set of assignments in the assignment matrix ($\mathcal{Z}$ in the formal analysis). ... For example, to calculate $\tau_{1x}(\alpha)$, we take the average over outcome values in graphs where node 1 is treated and subtract from it the average over outcome values in graphs where node 1 is under control.”

[Formal content] Fix a node $i$ and $d$ such that the normalizing constant $|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|$ (the $\zeta$-measure of the circle) is positive and finite, with $x \mapsto Y_x(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})$ $\zeta$-integrable on the circle for each of the finitely many $(z, \mathbf{z}_{-i})$.
(a) $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$ for $z \in \{0,1\}$.
(b) $\tau_i(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d} \tau_{ix}(\alpha)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$, and hence $\tau(d;\alpha) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{|\{x : d_i(x) = d\}|}\int_{x : d_i(x) = d}\tau_{ix}(\alpha)\,\mathrm{d}\zeta$.
(c) [Toy design.] If $N = 4$ and $\mathbf{Z}$ is uniform on $\{0,1\}^4$ (sixteen assignments with equal probability), then for every node $i$ and point $x$, $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha) = \frac18\sum_{\mathbf{z} \in \{0,1\}^4 :\, z_i = z} Y_x(\mathbf{z})$, so $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ is the mean of $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ over the eight assignments with $z_i = 1$ minus its mean over the eight assignments with $z_i = 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions (S1)–(S5): the spatial field $\mathcal{X}$, the nodes $x(i)$, the assignment $\mathbf{Z}$ with support $\mathcal{Z}$, potential outcomes $Y_x(\mathbf{z})$ (p. 141); $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ and $\tau_{ix}(\alpha)$ (p. 142); $d_i(x)$, $\mu_i(\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{z}); d)$, $\mu_i(z; d, \alpha)$, $\tau_i(d;\alpha)$, $\tau(d;\alpha)$ (p. 143); $\widehat{\tau}_{HA}(d)$, $N_1$, $N_0$ (p. 144). The toy example: (S8). Convention on the domain of the potential outcomes: (S9)(ii).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P008-H1 is the definition of the target quantity; its mathematical content is the two identities stated in words on p. 143 ((a), (b): a finite expectation commutes with the circle average) and the computing rule of Section 4 ((c)). Both fresh readers followed these steps and report them as holding (the caveat they attach is the scope question of P008-E001, not confirmed). (c) uses that under the uniform law on $\{0,1\}^4$ the law of $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ is uniform on $\{0,1\}^3$; for a design in which $Z_i$ and $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ are dependent the mean over the assignments with $z_i = z$ is a conditional mean and need not equal $Y_{ix}(z;\alpha)$ (P008-E001, not confirmed as an error: the paper does not assert that identity for other designs). The measurability and integrability conditions are added here; the paper says only that $\zeta$ is “a suitable integration measure”. The corrected display is P008-T14.
